items.text:
Below is the stimulus for question 30 a.

 

The following fragment of code used to represent RGB colours, is based on the object oriented programming (OOP) paradigm.

class Colour {

public int Red;

public int Green;

public int Blue;

private final String hexDigits = "0123456789ABCDEF";

public Colour() {

setValue(0, 0, 0);

}

public Colour(int r, int g, int b) {

setValue(r, g, b);

}

public int Value() {

return Red * 256 * 256 + Green * 256 + Blue;

}

public virtual void setValue(int r, int g, int b) {

Red = r;

Green = g;

Blue = b;

}

public virtual String ToHex() {

return FormatHex(Red) + FormatHex(Green) + FormatHex(Blue);

}

protected static String FormatHex(int v) {

int upper = v / 16;

int lower = v % 16; 

return hexDigits[upper].ToString() + hexDigits[lower].ToString();

}

}

class Colour

{

private int _green;

private int _blue;

public Colour() {

}

 

public Colour(int r, int g, int b) {

}

 

public int getRed() {

return _red;

}

 

public void setRed(int value) {

_red = getValidValue(value);

}

 

public int getGreen() {

return _green;

}

 

public void setGreen(int value) {

_green = getValidValue(value);

}

 

public int getBlue() {

return _blue;

}

 

public void setBlue(int value) {

_blue = getValidValue(value);

}

 

public int Value() {

return getRed() * 256 * 256 + getGreen() * 256 + getBlue();

}

 

public virtual void setValue(int r, int g, int b) {

setRed(r);

setGreen(g);

setBlue(b);

}

 

public virtual String ToHex() {

return FormatHex(getRed()) + FormatHex(getGreen()) + FormatHex(getBlue());

}

 

protected static String FormatHex(int value) {

int upper = value / 16;

int lower = value % 16;

return hexDigits[upper].ToString() + hexDigits[lower].ToString();

}

 

protected static int getValidValue(int value) {

if (value < 0)

return 0;

else if (value > 255)

return 255;

else

return value;

}

}

items.text:
The following statement briefly describes the differences between two different styles of programming : 

“Imperative” programming tells the computer how to do something, and as a result what you want to happen will happen, whereas “Declarative” programming tells the computer what you would like to happen, and lets the computer figure out how to do it.

Discuss the differences between these two approaches to programming. In your discussion, give examples of where each style of programming might be used.

criteria.criterion: Provides a good discussion on the differences between the two programming paradigms giving suitable examples where each might be used
Provides a discussion that shows understanding of differences between the two programming methodologies
Shows some understanding of either Imperative or Declarative programming methodologies beyond simply restating the question

sampleAnswerContentItem.text:
The choice of paradigm for software development usually revolve around the requirements of the software, the skill-set of the developers and environment into which the program is likely to placed.

Imperative programming is a paradigm which describes computation in terms of statements that change a program state whereas declarative programming expresses what the program should accomplish without prescribing how to do it in terms of sequences of actions to be taken. An example of imperative programming style is Procedural programming in which the program is built from one or more procedures (functions or subroutines). Many low level languages use imperative style and many commonly used languages such as C++ use this style of program. Other types of programming paradigms such as OOP can also be considered a being Imperative programming types.

Declarative programming is a style of building the structure and elements of computer programs, that expresses the logic of a computation without describing its control flow. An example of declarative programming styles is logical programming languages. Logic programming deals with the relationship with data without specifying how this is actually achieved. An example of this language is Prolog and is used for building up relationships between facts and rules.

markingRubricContentItem.text: Encapsulation is the process of hiding an object’s data and methods within the object by making them private. Only those methods required to use the object are exposed  publicly to form an interface for programmers to use. Encapsulation creates a self contained class that can be reused with confidence. The interface can remain the same  even when the inner working are improved.

items.text: When designing objects, why not make all attributes and methods public? Discuss.

criteria.criterion: Good discussion of public versus private
Sound discussion of public versus private
Limited understanding of public versus private

markingRubricContentItem.text:
If all attributes are made public then users (programmers) will be able to change the  value of any attribute at will to any value they wish. For instance they could alter a  counter that keeps track of the number of items sold. By making attributes private  such errors cannot occur. it is better to use a public method for all input data so that  the method can validate the data. 

In terms of methods, which process data in attributes, there will be some methods that should be public, namely those that obtain input and those that display output. Other  processing methods within the object should be private particularly if they do are  subprocesses within a larger process. If all methods were public then users of the  objects could execute methods inappropristely.

items.text: Discuss how the productivity of programmers is affected by the programming paradigm that has been chosen to solve a problem.

criteria.criterion: Provides a detailed thorough discussion regarding paradigms and the  productivity of programmers.
Provides a good discussion regarding paradigms and the productivity of  programmers.
Provides a discussion about the features of different programming paradigms.
Identifies a feature of a programming paradigm.

markingRubricContentItem.text:
• Speed of code generation: the speed at which the developer can write code which  solves a particular problem is heavily influenced by the chosen programming  paradigm. Different problems are suited to different paradigms. For example, a  book cataloguing system would be well suited to an object-oriented paradigm since  it has many abstract entities (i.e. books) which need to be represented somehow  (such as objects) in the program. 

  • Approach to testing: the choice of paradigm has an influence on how easily  programs can be tested. Unit testing is often used in object-oriented programming  to test individual modules of code. This is very efficient as each module can be  tested in isolation as they are self-contained, also allowing modules to easy be re tested after they are changed or modified. 

  • Effect on maintenance: adopting paradigms which require the modularisation of  code makes maintenance easier through ease of locating and isolating sections of  code. 

  • Efficiency of solution once coded: higher-level languages (such as object-oriented  languages) are often less efficient to run than pure imperative languages. While  they may be more efficient to execute, they may not be more efficient in term of  the programmer’s time to code and maintain. 

  • Learning curve: it is difficult and time consuming to learn languages based around  new paradigms.

items.text: Compare the direct cut-over conversion method with the pilot conversion method when implementing a new or updated system.

criteria.criterion: Provides THREE quality differences between the direct cut-over and the pilot conversion  methods

sampleAnswerContentItem.text:
The direct cut-over approach is a direct approach where old system is cut and over write by new system. The direct cutover approach causes the changeover from the old system to the new system to occur immediately when the new system becomes operational. 

This is a least expensive method among all four but involves high risk of data loss. With the direct cutover method, company cannot revert to the old system as a backup option.

Direct cutover involves more risks of a total system failure.

The pilot conversion method involves implementing the complete new system at a selected location of the company. The group that uses the new system first is called the pilot site. The old system continues to operate for the entire organization including the pilot site. After the system proves successful at the pilot site, it is implemented in the rest of the organization.

Pilot site assures the working of the new system and reduces the risk of system failure.

markingGuidanceContentItem.text:
Authentication and authorisation are two fundamental concepts in the field of security in software engineering, and while they are often used together, they serve distinct purposes.

Authentication is the process of verifying the identity of a user or system. It ensures that individuals or entities are who they claim to be before granting access to resources or systems. Common methods of authentication include the use of usernames and passwords, biometric verification (such as fingerprints or facial recognition), and multi-factor authentication (MFA), which combines multiple verification methods. For instance, when a user logs into their email account by entering their username and password, the system performs authentication to confirm that the user is legitimate and allowed to access that account.

On the other hand, authorisation is the process that determines what an authenticated user is allowed to do within a system. Once a user's identity has been verified through authentication, authorisation governs their access rights and permissions to various resources or functionalities. For example, in a company’s internal database, a manager may have the authorisation to view and modify employee records, while a regular employee might only have the authorisation to view their own record. Authorisation ensures that users can only perform actions that they are permitted to do, thereby protecting sensitive data and maintaining system integrity.

markingGuidanceContentItem.text:
Collaboration is essential in software engineering, as it significantly enhances the efficiency and quality of software development projects. Effective collaboration can yield several key advantages, including improved problem-solving, enhanced communication, and increased productivity.

Firstly, collaboration fosters improved problem-solving. When team members work together, they can share diverse perspectives and expertise, leading to innovative solutions to complex problems. For instance, a developer may encounter a challenging bug within the code. By collaborating with colleagues, they can brainstorm potential fixes and draw on each other’s experiences, resulting in faster resolution and enhanced code quality.

Secondly, enhanced communication is a critical benefit of collaboration. Open channels of communication ensure that all team members are on the same page regarding project goals, requirements, and progress. This transparency helps to reduce misunderstandings and misalignments, which can lead to costly errors down the line. Regular meetings, discussions, and updates create an environment where team members can express concerns and provide feedback openly.

Lastly, collaboration can lead to increased productivity. When developers work together, they can divide tasks based on individual strengths and expertise. This division of labour enables the team to tackle multiple components of a project simultaneously, reducing development time and accelerating the delivery of the final product. Additionally, collaborative tools streamline workflows, allowing team members to track progress and manage tasks more efficiently.

A prime example of a collaboration tool used in software development is GitHub. GitHub is a platform that allows developers to host and review code, manage projects, and collaborate with others. It facilitates collaboration through features like pull requests, which enable team members to propose changes to the codebase and allow for peer review before merging those changes. This process not only enhances code quality through collective review but also provides a clear record of changes and discussions, fostering better communication among developers.
